Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah)
feest uv ded-i-KAY-shun
noun phrase (biblical feast)
From the Hebrew Chanukkah ("dedication"); Greek enkainia ("renewal, dedication") at John 10:22. Commemorates the rededication of the temple after its defilement, in the second century BC.

Biblical Definition

The Feast of Dedication (Hebrew Chanukkah, "dedication") is the Jewish festival commemorating the rededication of the temple in Jerusalem after its defilement by the Syrian-Greek tyrant Antiochus IV Epiphanes, in the events of the Maccabean revolt (c. 167-164 BC). Antiochus had desecrated the temple, erecting an altar to Zeus and sacrificing swine upon it — the "abomination of desolation" foreshadowed in Daniel. The Maccabees, led by Judas Maccabeus, rose in revolt, recovered Jerusalem, cleansed the temple, and rededicated the altar; the eight-day festival of Dedication commemorates that cleansing and rededication. Though the institution of the feast falls in the intertestamental period (recorded in 1 and 2 Maccabees, which the dictionary holds as historically valuable but not canonical Scripture), the feast itself appears once in the canonical New Testament: "And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter. And Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon's porch" (John 10:22-23). The Lord Jesus was present at the temple during the very feast that celebrated the temple's cleansing and rededication — and there He declared Himself one with the Father (John 10:30), the true temple and the true light. The setting is rich with significance: at the feast commemorating the rededicated house of God, the One who is greater than the temple stood in it. The Feast of Dedication reminds the church of God's faithfulness in preserving His worship through times of persecution and desecration, and it points beyond every earthly temple to Christ, in whom the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily (Col 2:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

The Jewish festival (Hebrew Chanukkah, "dedication") commemorating the rededication of the temple after Antiochus IV's defilement, in the Maccabean revolt (c. 164 BC); appears once in canon at John 10:22, where the Lord Jesus, present at the feast, declared Himself one with the Father.

FEAST OF DEDICATION (HANUKKAH), noun phrase. Hebrew Chanukkah ("dedication"); Greek enkainia (John 10:22).

Commemorates the rededication of the temple after its defilement by Antiochus IV Epiphanes, in the Maccabean revolt (c. 167-164 BC).

Antiochus had set up an altar to Zeus and sacrificed swine (the "abomination of desolation"); the Maccabees cleansed and rededicated the temple.

An eight-day festival; instituted in the intertestamental period (1 and 2 Maccabees, historically valuable but not canonical).

Appears once in canon: the Lord Jesus was at the temple during the feast (John 10:22-23) and declared Himself one with the Father (John 10:30).

Key Scripture

John 10:22-23 — "And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter. And Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon's porch."

John 10:30 — "I and my Father are one."

Daniel 11:31 — "And arms shall stand on his part, and they shall pollute the sanctuary of strength, and shall take away the daily sacrifice, and they shall place the abomination that maketh desolate."

Colossians 2:9 — "For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily."

Modern Corruption

The Feast of Dedication is corrupted when its intertestamental sources are wrongly elevated to canon or wrongly dismissed as worthless, when its appearance in John 10 is overlooked, or when the providential preservation of true worship it celebrates is forgotten.

expand to see more

Canon-confusion. The institution of the Feast of Dedication is recorded in 1 and 2 Maccabees, books of the Apocrypha. Two opposite errors arise: Rome and the Eastern churches treat these books as canonical Scripture (a position the Reformation rejected, holding the Hebrew canon); some Protestants, reacting, dismiss them as worthless. The Reformed position is the careful middle: the books of the Maccabees are NOT canonical Scripture and bind no conscience as God's Word, but they are historically valuable accounts of the intertestamental period that illuminate the world into which Christ came. The feast they record is not commanded in canonical Scripture, yet the canonical Gospel of John notes the Lord's presence at it — a fact worth weighing.

John-10-setting overlooked. Readers often pass over the note that the Lord's great declaration of unity with the Father (John 10:30) came at the Feast of Dedication, in winter, in the temple (John 10:22-23). The setting is no accident: at the very feast celebrating the cleansing and rededication of the house of God, the One who is the true temple, in whom the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily (Col 2:9), stood in the temple and claimed oneness with the Father. The feast that looked back to a purified house pointed forward to the Holy One standing in it. To read John 10 without the feast's significance is to miss a layer of the Gospel's design.
